items.title: Analysts in regulated firms can query private databases with a 321B-class model on one desk
items.connection: The 2.48 bpw quants put a 321B-class MoE on one DGX Spark, datasette-llm can call any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and llama.cpp's new slot scheduler and prompt hashing target exactly this kind of shared local server.
items.context: many firms cannot send internal data to third-party APIs
chain: A 321B-class agentic MoE now fits in about 96.5 GiB on one 128GB box with about 95% top-1 agreement.
Datasette plugins can point at a local OpenAI-compatible server with no code changes.
A slot scheduler and prompt running hash in llama.cpp suggest several analysts can share one server, with repeated schema prompts possibly reused.
Data teams that were blocked from cloud LLMs can pilot natural-language exploration of sensitive tables without a procurement fight.
items.who: Analytics leads in banks, insurers and health systems benefit; the data platform or compliance budget pays for one desktop box.
items.variable: time from question to first usable query on restricted data
items.versus: Doing nothing leaves restricted data outside LLM tooling, and hosted assistants fail the data residency review.
items.smallest_test: Serve one quant behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, connect datasette-llm, and have 3 analysts run 30 real questions on a sanitized copy; success is 70% correct answers with no request leaving the box.
items.disconfirm: The quant cannot be served through an OpenAI-compatible server at usable speed, or answers on real schemas are mostly wrong.

items.title: Engineering teams can require a design review sign-off before any coding agent writes code
items.connection: LoopForge sequences Codex, Claude Code and CodeBuddy with human approval gates, Google's elephant-goldfish-model supports agent-assisted design review, and Plannotator adds human review loops, so the gate can sit at the design stage instead of only at the diff.
items.context: code review is the main bottleneck when agents produce large diffs
chain: LoopForge gives one self-hosted place to script several coding agents with sign-off steps.
A design review step and a human plan review can be placed as the first gate, before implementation agents run.
Bad approaches get rejected when they cost a paragraph, not a large diff.
Reviewer time shifts from reading code to approving plans, which scales better as teams add agents.
items.who: Engineering managers running several coding agents benefit; platform teams pay in setup time on a self-hosted tool.
items.variable: share of agent pull requests rejected after review
items.versus: Gating only at the pull request wastes agent runs and reviewer hours on work that was wrong from the plan.
items.smallest_test: Run 20 tickets through LoopForge with a design review gate and 20 without; success is at least 25% fewer rejected pull requests in the gated group.
items.disconfirm: Gated and ungated tickets have the same rejection rate, or reviewers rubber-stamp plans.

items.context: security teams resist unattended agent access to internal systems
chain: The earlier idea risked rejection because security teams would not trust an agent with staging access.
LoopForge scripts the debug run and stops for a human sign-off before any fix is proposed or merged.
Context-mode sandboxes tool output so long debugging sessions stay within context.
A gated, logged workflow is something a security review can approve, so the idea moves from demo to pilot.
items.who: QA leads and platform teams benefit; engineering budget pays for setup and agent usage.
items.variable: time from staging bug report to verified fix
items.versus: Ungated agent access gets refused by security, and manual debugging keeps the current backlog.
items.smallest_test: Run 15 known staging bugs through a gated LoopForge flow; success is security sign-off on the design and at least 8 correct diagnoses approved at the gate.
items.disconfirm: Security still refuses the tunnel with gates in place, or reviewers reject most agent diagnoses.

For a buyer, models of this size now run on one desktop box instead of a server. The OSWorld and tool-use gains cited for these models are upstream figures and were not retested on the quants.

items.body: That format makes a new open text-to-image model easier to run on your own machine, and the files have 127,803 downloads. It fits the same push toward running capable models without a hosted service. No quality or speed figures exist for these quants, so test them before you rely on them.
